sources.title: William W. Hager, Runge-Kutta methods in optimal control and the transformed adjoint system, Numerische Mathematik 87 (2000)
sources.locator: Complete 36-page paper inspected; §1 order-condition caveat; §2 Runge–Kutta stage equations, State Uniqueness Property, Theorem 2.1; §3 transformed adjoint system and Proposition 3.1.

contents.name: §2 State Uniqueness Property: local smooth Runge–Kutta stage branch under a small-step implicit-function hypothesis
contents.reason: The item proves its own branch derivative from a contractive stage ball and a nonsingular residual Jacobian; Hager supplies context for the stage equations, not the local branch proof.

contents.name: §2, Table 1 and Theorem 2.1: optimal-control convergence conditions and error estimate
contents.reason: The DIF3 gradient-error theorem assumes separate state, adjoint, derivative-data, endpoint, and quadrature bounds; it does not assert Hager's optimal-control convergence theorem or its stronger positivity and coercivity hypotheses.

contents.name: §3 transformed adjoint system and Proposition 3.1: equivalence of the transformed first-order conditions
contents.reason: The local finite-graph proof derives the exact reverse recursion for arbitrary C1 step maps; the Runge–Kutta control setting is retained only as context.

contents.name: §1 and §3, Remark 3.2: the discrete objective gradient is computed from the transformed first-order system, while its RK adjoint scheme can differ from the state scheme
contents.reason: The local theorem makes the discrete/continuous distinction explicit and supplies its own augmented error assumptions instead of importing Hager's method-specific conditions.

sources.title: Michael B. Giles and Niles A. Pierce, An Introduction to the Adjoint Approach to Design, complete author/coauthor-hosted 23-page PDF
sources.locator: Complete 23-page paper inspected; §2.4 discrete sensitivity and adjoint system; §3.1 continuous PDE adjoint and boundary conditions; §3.6 and §4 discrete/continuous gradient distinction.

contents.name: §2.4 duality formulation: the discrete sensitivity equation and transposed adjoint produce the same objective derivative
contents.reason: The finite-graph proof establishes this identity for arbitrary differentiable step maps and includes direct parameter terms that the CFD-specific derivation does not cover.

contents.name: §3.1 duality and the adjoint PDE: integration by parts determines the adjoint operator and boundary conditions
contents.reason: The local variational theorem states and proves the transposed-form adjoint identity under operator-norm C1 and uniform coercivity hypotheses, without importing CFD boundary conditions.

contents.name: §3.6 and §4: a continuous adjoint discretization need not equal the derivative of the discrete objective at finite resolution
contents.reason: The counterexample gives an explicit C1 family with uniform state convergence and unbounded derivative error, and the ODE estimate lists the additional adjoint and derivative-data assumptions.

contents.name: §§5–6 aircraft-design applications and CFD implementation comparisons
contents.reason: The assigned examples are finite scalar, ODE shooting, elliptic diffusion, and QR calculations; no aerodynamic geometry, Euler/Navier–Stokes discretization, or aircraft design claim is made.

alternatives.argument: Its local proof differentiates each finite state step, applies the reverse accumulation rule, and telescopes the tangent-cotangent identity; the finite-graph claim is proved from the declared AD and chain-rule suppliers.
Its local proof differentiates the uniformly coercive variational state, solves the transposed variational adjoint, and substitutes the two equations; it uses no Giles-specific CFD assumptions.
The counterexample directly bounds h^2 sin(theta/h^3) uniformly by h^2 and computes its derivative at zero as 1/h, independently of any source statement.

sources.title: Hannes Meinlschmidt, Optimization with Partial Differential Equations, complete lecture notes (2023)
sources.locator: Complete 65-page lecture notes inspected; §1.1 reduced control-to-state map; Examples 3.38–3.39 on semilinear elliptic KKT and adjoint equations.

contents.name: §1.1 reduced problem and control-to-state operator: a unique state can be eliminated to define a reduced objective
contents.reason: The assigned definition fixes a parameterized weak elliptic state and reduced objective but deliberately makes no existence or optimization assertion.

contents.name: Example 3.38: KKT system for a semilinear elliptic boundary-control problem
contents.reason: DIF3 treats unconstrained finite-dimensional parameters in a uniformly coercive linear variational state family; this constrained semilinear boundary-control KKT system is not its claim.

contents.name: Example 3.39: elliptic adjoint equation and reduced control gradient in weak form
contents.reason: The local theorem proves the parameterized nonsymmetric coercive-form formula directly; the lecture-note example is a separately structured optimal-control treatment.

sources.title: Christian Clason, Introduction to Finite Element Methods, complete lecture notes, arXiv:1709.08618v2
sources.locator: Complete 118-page lecture notes inspected; §1.2 Ritz–Galerkin approximation and Aubin–Nitsche duality; §11.1 trace and integration-by-parts results; §11.2 parabolic variational equation; §12.1 method-of-lines finite-element semidiscretization.

contents.name: §1.2 Ritz–Galerkin approximation: Galerkin orthogonality and the energy-norm best-approximation estimate
contents.reason: The local finite-element gradient theorem invokes the exact conforming estimate only to supply state and adjoint energy bounds, then proves a separate derivative-data error budget.

contents.name: §1.2 duality argument (Aubin–Nitsche): extra dual regularity and dual approximation improve the L2 state rate
contents.reason: The local corollary applies the stated L2 rates to both state and adjoint and separately assumes L2-bounded parameter derivative maps and their consistency defects.

contents.name: Theorem 11.1 and Lemma 11.2: the evolution-space trace and time integration-by-parts identity
contents.reason: The conditional adjoint proof uses the energy-space pairing identity but assumes state differentiability and adjoint existence instead of claiming parabolic well-posedness.

contents.name: Theorem 11.3: existence, uniqueness, and energy bound for a parabolic variational solution
contents.reason: The assigned parabolic sensitivity theorem is conditional on a differentiable state and an adjoint; it does not claim existence or uniqueness of either solution.

contents.name: §12.1 method of lines: spatial finite-element discretization gives a finite-dimensional parabolic ODE
contents.reason: The source supplies semidiscrete finite-element context; the local gradient estimate uses the assigned Ritz residual theorem and includes the time-dependent projection derivative explicitly.

contents.name: §12.2 space-time continuous and discontinuous Galerkin methods and their time-discrete error estimates
contents.reason: The assigned parabolic gradient estimate is semidiscrete in time and makes no cG/dG time-discretization or fully discrete convergence-rate claim.

sources.title: Predrag Cvitanović et al., ChaosBook, Chapter 6: Lyapunov exponents, version 15
sources.locator: Complete 11-page Chapter 6 inspected; §6.2 QR scheme, geometric d-volume interpretation, and Remark 6.3 on numerical Lyapunov calculations.

contents.name: §6.2 QR scheme: the d-dimensional parallelepiped volume is the product of the diagonal entries of R
contents.reason: The local theorem proves the exact finite-product identity by determinant telescoping and adds its own conditioning-dependent logarithm error bound.

contents.name: Remark 6.3: Gram–Schmidt vectors need not be covariant tangent directions and Lyapunov computations involve further numerical choices
contents.reason: The example is deliberately a finite QR determinant calculation and makes no infinite-time exponent or covariant-vector claim.

contents.name: §6.2 asymptotic Lyapunov spectrum and long-time interpretation
contents.reason: DIF3 adds an exact finite-time volume identity only; it asserts no ergodic limit, Lyapunov exponent, shadowing, or asymptotic tangent-direction result.
